title: What a Court Minority Can Actually Force
hook: A losing bloc on a court can write a blistering dissent, or it can hold a procedural lever. Only one of those changes what the court does.
key_points: Courts decide by majority, so minority influence has to come from procedural rules rather than from votes on the merits.
The Supreme Court's main such rule is the Rule of Four: four justices can grant certiorari and put a case on the docket over the majority's preference.
Below four, a minority has only expression — a dissent from denial of certiorari carries no binding force.
Writing at SCOTUSblog, Josh Blackman proposes a set of Rules of Three giving three justices procedural powers.

His examples include a chief justice supplying a courtesy fourth vote for cert, three justices forcing disclosure of how colleagues voted on cert denials and emergency applications, and three justices requiring a prompt conference or oral argument on emergency-docket matters.
Blackman argues such levers would trade performative dissents for real consequences; the underlying question is how much minority procedural power a majoritarian institution can absorb.
content_html: On any court that decides by majority, the losing side has no power over the result. What it can sometimes have is power over process: which cases get heard, how fast, and how visibly. That distinction is the whole subject of court-reform debates that never touch the merits of a single case.
extra_html: The Supreme Court's best-known example is the Rule of Four: it takes five votes to win a case but only four to grant certiorari, so a bloc that expects to lose can still force the Court to take an issue up. Below four, the minority has expression alone — a dissent from denial of certiorari is read widely and binds no one. Writing at SCOTUSblog, law professor Josh Blackman proposes extending procedural power downward with what he calls Rules of Three: among them, a chief justice supplying a courtesy fourth vote when three colleagues want review; three justices being able to require that the votes on cert denials and emergency applications be made public; and three justices being able to force a prompt conference, or oral argument, on emergency-docket matters. Blackman's argument is that giving a minority real levers would replace "performative" dissents with choices that carry consequences. Whether or not the specific proposals are wise, they frame a question that recurs across institutions from courts to legislatures: how much procedural power can a majority-rule body hand its minority before the majority stops being able to govern? (This card describes the U.S. Supreme Court specifically, and summarizes one commentator's proposal rather than adopted rules.)

related.title: The Power of a Dissent
related.hook: A dissenting judge loses the case — but a sharp dissent can outlive the majority, persuading future courts or pushing lawmakers to rewrite the rule.

related.title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
related.hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: The Supreme Court's 'Shadow Docket'
related.hook: Most Supreme Court rulings today aren't fully-argued opinions — they're fast, often unsigned orders with little explanation. In the term ending October 2025, those quietly became the majority.

flashcards.prompt: What is the Rule of Four?
flashcards.back_html: The Supreme Court's practice that four justices can grant certiorari, putting a case on the docket even though five would be needed to win it — a minority power over the agenda, not the outcome.

flashcards.prompt: Why must minority influence on a court come from procedural rules rather than merits votes?

choices.text: Outcomes are decided by majority, so the only lever a minority can hold is over process and agenda
Dissenting justices are barred from voting on the merits
Procedural rules require unanimous agreement to apply

flashcards.explanation_html: A minority cannot win a case by definition. It can sometimes decide which cases get heard, and how quickly.

flashcards.prompt: What kind of powers does Blackman's Rules of Three proposal contemplate?

choices.text: Letting three justices force disclosure of votes, or a prompt conference or argument on emergency matters
Letting three justices overturn a majority ruling on the merits
Letting three justices appoint additional colleagues

flashcards.explanation_html: Every item is procedural — agenda, timing, transparency — not a way to change who wins the case.
